_comment: // DRAFT: needs human accuracy review. Hybrid theme: a taken-over recipe as a stand-in for undocumented code. Gates now also test the RAG terms taught in Learn (chunking, embedding, retrieval, generation).

questions.q: You took over a recipe with no notes. Fastest way?
questions.explain: PRISM reads the whole recipe book and answers in plain English, just like it does for code nobody documented.

questions.q: You took over the recipe. First move?
questions.explain: Start by asking. PRISM gives you the big picture in minutes, whether it's a stall or a system.

questions.q: Customer asks what's in the chilli. You?
questions.explain: PRISM answers and points to the exact line it read, so your answer holds up. Same for questions about code.

questions.q: Only Uncle knows the sauce. He's away. Now what?
questions.explain: When the only expert is away, PRISM still knows what the notes say. No more single point of failure.

questions.q: Nobody knows why the recipe adds sugar. Quickest answer?
questions.explain: Ask PRISM why a step exists and it shows the line that explains it, before you delete a rule that matters.

questions.q: The recipe book is huge. What does PRISM do first?
questions.explain: That's CHUNKING: the book, or the codebase, is cut into small pieces so PRISM can later pull just the part it needs.

questions.q: What does RAG stand for?
questions.explain: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: first retrieve the pieces that match your question, then generate the answer from them.
questions.citation: PRISM user guide · what is RAG

questions.q: Code can't leave the office. Why is PRISM okay?
questions.explain: PRISM runs on the intranet, so your code never leaves.

questions.q: Want less salt. Unsure what it affects?
questions.explain: Before changing one ingredient, ask PRISM which steps depend on it, just like checking what a code change affects.

questions.q: Which question should you ask PRISM?
questions.explain: Specific questions get specific, cited answers, about recipes or about code.

questions.q: Which question gets a useful answer?
questions.explain: Ask about one step and PRISM points to the exact line. Vague in, vague out.

questions.q: Which question is clearest?
questions.explain: A clear question about one step gets a clear answer, with its source.

questions.q: You want to master the rice. Ask PRISM:
questions.explain: Name the thing you care about and PRISM traces every step that touches it.

questions.q: How does PRISM know which pieces to pick?
questions.explain: That's EMBEDDING: every piece is filed by meaning, and so is your question. PRISM picks the pieces closest in meaning to what you asked.

questions.q: You ask a question. What happens to it first?
questions.explain: Your question is embedded the same way as the pieces, so PRISM can match it against them.

questions.q: PRISM works best when you ask:
questions.explain: One clear question at a time gets the sharpest answer.

questions.q: You ask 'spicy'. Notes say 'lots of chilli'. Found?
questions.explain: PRISM matches meaning, not exact keywords, so 'spicy' finds the chilli step. Ask about 'tax rate' and it finds the code that works it out, whatever it's named.

questions.q: First answer was too broad. Next step?
questions.explain: Follow-ups narrow it down, like zooming from the whole recipe to one step, or from a system to one file.

questions.q: Which answer can you trust?
questions.explain: An answer with an exact source is one you can check yourself.

questions.q: PRISM pulls only the matching pieces. That step is?
questions.explain: That's RETRIEVAL: out of the whole book, or the whole codebase, PRISM pulls only the pieces that match your question.

questions.q: Why does PRISM show its sources?
questions.explain: Sources let you verify every answer, so you never have to take it on faith.

questions.q: An answer with no source is...
questions.explain: No source means you can't check it yet. Treat it as a claim.

questions.q: Two answers sound right. Which do you trust?
questions.explain: Confidence isn't evidence. The one that cites its source wins.

questions.q: PRISM writes its answer from what?
questions.explain: That's GENERATION: the answer is written from the retrieved pieces, so every claim can point back to its source.

questions.q: Health inspector asks how you store chicken. Best reply?
questions.explain: Inspectors and auditors want sources. PRISM gives you the exact step to show them.

questions.q: The answer cites a step. Smart next move?
questions.explain: Open the cited line and check it. That's the whole point of sources.

questions.q: Why is a RAG answer easy to check?
questions.explain: A RAG answer comes from pieces PRISM actually retrieved, so it can show you which ones. A chatbot answering from memory can't.

questions.q: Auditor asks how your prices are calculated. Who helps?
questions.explain: PRISM explains how a figure is worked out and cites where, for stall prices or for code.

questions.q: New helper starts today. What gets them cooking fastest?
questions.explain: New starters ask PRISM in plain English and get productive in days, in a kitchen or on a codebase.

questions.q: Who can use PRISM?
questions.explain: If you can ask a question, you can use PRISM. No coding or cooking degree needed.

questions.q: Why can't general AI chat tools explain your code?
questions.explain: A general AI tool hasn't read your codebase, so it can only guess. PRISM retrieves from your actual code before it answers.

questions.q: Customer asks: any peanuts in this? You?
questions.explain: When getting it wrong matters, check the cited source. Allergens or tax rules, same idea.

questions.q: Chunk, embed, retrieve... what comes next?
questions.explain: After retrieval comes GENERATION: PRISM writes the answer from the pieces it pulled and shows its sources.
questions.citation: PRISM user guide · how it works

questions.q: Inspector asks where a step is written. You show:
questions.explain: Show the exact page and line. Reviewers trust what they can check.

questions.q: Which step happens before retrieval?
questions.explain: Pieces are embedded first, filed by meaning, so retrieval can match them to your question. Generation comes last.
questions.citation: PRISM user guide · how it works

questions.q: Food critic asks why the rice smells so good. You?
questions.explain: PRISM traces cause to effect across steps, like tracing how code produced a result.
